explanations.explanation: God tells Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, the priest: “Say to the Israelites…” (Leviticus 15:2). So the whole people get this message, not a select few. No one in that camp gets to say they never heard about it. I think that's a pretty fair way to run things.

I get why you'd lean that way, since Aaron is a priest himself. But God says, “Say to the Israelites…” and that's the whole people. Moses and Aaron are the messengers, and everyone in the camp is the audience. This one isn't a priests-only meeting.

Elders don't show up in this passage at all. God tells Moses and Aaron, “Say to the Israelites…” (Leviticus 15:2). That means every Israelite is meant to hear it. The message goes out to the whole camp, no VIP section.

That's exactly what God says: “…the discharge is unclean.” (Leviticus 15:2). He doesn't call it a curse or a punishment. He names it unclean and then spells out what to do about it. Clear words, clear steps. I like a clear recipe.

God never uses that word here. What He says is, “…the discharge is unclean.” (Leviticus 15:2). Unclean is the word the passage uses, over and over. And every time it comes with a plan for what to do next.

God doesn't wave this one off. He says the discharge is unclean, and then He gives a whole list of what that touches. Harmless things don't come with this much laundry. Everything in the passage treats it as something to take seriously.

explanations.answer: Wash his clothes and bathe with water
explanations.explanation: Right there in verse 5: “Anyone who touches his bed must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” So it's a wash, a bath, and then a wait until evening. That's the whole list. It's not a big production, just a clear one.

explanations.answer: Shave off all his hair and his beard
explanations.explanation: No razors in this passage. Verse 5 says the person “must wash his clothes and bathe with water.” Then he's unclean until evening. Your barber can stay booked for the week.

explanations.answer: Stay outside the camp for a whole week
explanations.explanation: A whole week is a lot longer than what verse 5 says. The person who touches the bed washes his clothes, bathes, and “will be unclean until evening.” That's one day's end, not seven. Nobody has to pack a tent over touching a bed.
Not quite. Verse 9 says, “Any saddle on which the man with the discharge rides will be unclean.” So the saddle doesn't stay clean. The uncleanness goes with him, even onto the animal's back.

Right, it's false. Verse 9 says, “Any saddle on which the man with the discharge rides will be unclean.” Beds, furniture, and now saddles. The list keeps growing, and you can bet nobody borrowed his saddle for a quick ride.

explanations.answer: When he didn't rinse his hands first
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the key word is “without.” Verse 11 says, “If the man with the discharge touches anyone without first rinsing his hands with water, the one who was touched must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” So the rinse is what matters. Rinsed hands first, and the verse doesn't send that person to the washtub.

explanations.answer: When he touched them after dark
explanations.explanation: The time of day isn't in this verse at all. Verse 11 is about one thing: whether he rinsed his hands with water before touching. If he didn't, the person he touched must wash his clothes and bathe. Sundown doesn't change a thing.

explanations.answer: When he touched them on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath doesn't come up in this passage. Verse 11 puts it on whether the man rinsed his hands first. If he touches someone “without first rinsing his hands with water,” that person washes and bathes. It's about the hands, not the calendar.
Verse 12 says, “Any clay pot that the man with the discharge touches must be broken…” Ouch. Clay pots had a rough day in that camp. Nobody threw a party for the pot.
Close, but rinsing is for a different item. Verse 12 says the wooden utensil “must be rinsed with water.” The clay pot “must be broken.” Same law, two different fates.
Nobody's digging a hole in this verse. It says plainly that any clay pot he touches “must be broken.” Burying isn't mentioned anywhere in the passage. Break it, and you're done.

Not this time. Verse 12 splits the two: the clay pot “must be broken,” but “any wooden utensil must be rinsed with water.” So the wooden one gets to stay in one piece. A rinse and it's back in business.
Right, it's false. Verse 12 says the clay pot must be broken, but the wooden utensil “must be rinsed with water.” Two materials, two instructions. The wooden spoon gets off easy.
Yes. Verse 13 says he must “bathe himself in fresh water, and he shall be clean.” So the passage names the water, and that's the end of it. Seven days counted, clothes washed, fresh water, clean.
No oil in this bath. Verse 13 says he must “bathe himself in fresh water, and he shall be clean.” Water is the only thing the passage names. Save the oil for something else.
That sounds fancy, but it's not in the verse. Verse 13 says he bathes “in fresh water.” Plain water, and then he shall be clean. Sometimes the simple answer is the right one.

Yes. Verse 14 says he is to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, come before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, “and give them to the priest.” The priest is the one who carries it from there. The man's job is to show up with the birds.

Moses is Israel's leader, and he's the one God speaks to here. But verse 14 says the birds are given “to the priest.” So the handoff happens at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, to the priest. Moses is the messenger in this passage, not the one receiving the birds.

The elders don't appear anywhere in this passage. Verse 14 says the man comes to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and gives the birds “to the priest.” That's the whole chain. One man, two birds, one priest.

explanations.answer: A sin offering and a burnt offering
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 15 says, “The priest is to sacrifice them, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering.” One bird for each. Then the verse says the priest “will make atonement for the man before the LORD because of his discharge.”

explanations.answer: A guilt offering and a grain offering
explanations.explanation: Those two aren't in this verse. Verse 15 says one bird is “a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering.” And a grain offering isn't even a bird. Two birds, two offerings, and those are the two.

explanations.answer: A peace offering and a wave offering
explanations.explanation: Neither of those is named here. Verse 15 says the priest sacrifices the two birds, “one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering.” That's how he makes atonement for the man before the LORD. Stick with those two names.

Not for this case. Verse 16 says only that the man “must bathe his whole body with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” The two birds on the eighth day belong to the man with a discharge (verses 13 to 15). This one is a bath and a wait until evening.

Right, it's false. For an emission of semen, verse 16 says the man “must bathe his whole body with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” No eighth day, no birds. The birds belong to the discharge case before it.

Not quite. Verse 18 says, “If a man lies with a woman and there is an emission of semen, both must bathe with water, and they will remain unclean until evening.” Both of them, not just the man. So the bath is for two.
Right, it's false. Verse 18 says, “…both must bathe with water, and they will remain unclean until evening.” So the woman bathes too, and both are unclean until evening. The law counts them together.

Yes. Verse 19 says, “…she will be unclean due to her menstruation for seven days, and anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening.” Seven is the number for this one. The passage doesn't hand out numbers carelessly.
Three is a bit short. Verse 19 says she “will be unclean due to her menstruation for seven days.” Seven is the number the passage gives. Count again, friend.
Forty is way more than the text says. Verse 19 says she “will be unclean due to her menstruation for seven days.” Seven days, not forty. That would be a very long wait for a very short verse.

Yes. Verse 19 says, “…anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening.” That's for the person who touches her, and it ends at evening. It's the same waiting time you've seen all through this passage.

explanations.answer: They bring two birds to the priest
explanations.explanation: The birds come later, and for someone else. Verse 19 says the person who touches her “will be unclean until evening.” The two birds in this passage come on the eighth day after a woman is cleansed (verses 28 to 30). Touching her doesn't send anyone to the Tent of Meeting.
Nobody is sent out of camp in this verse. Verse 19 says, “…anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening.” That's all it says. They stay put and wait for evening.

Not this time. Until evening is for someone who touches her or her things. Verse 24 says, “If a man lies with her and her menstrual flow touches him, he will be unclean for seven days, and any bed on which he lies will become unclean.” That's seven days, a lot longer than one evening.

Right, it's false. Verse 24 says, “…he will be unclean for seven days, and any bed on which he lies will become unclean.” So it's seven days, not just until evening. The bed he lies on is unclean too.

explanations.answer: All the days of her discharge
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 25 says, “…she will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge, just as she is during the days of her menstruation.” So there's no set number here. It lasts as long as the discharge does.

Seven is the number for her regular period, and for counting after she is cleansed. For this kind of discharge, verse 25 says she “will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge.” So the number depends on how long it lasts. The seven days come after it ends (verse 28).

Until evening is for people who touch her bed or her furniture (verse 27). For her, verse 25 says she “will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge.” So it lasts as long as the discharge does, not just one evening.

explanations.answer: So they don't die by making His tabernacle unclean
explanations.explanation: Yes, and this is where God finally says it outright. Verse 31: “You must keep the children of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them.” So it's about His tabernacle, and it's serious. This is the reason behind all that washing.

explanations.answer: So sickness doesn't spread from tent to tent
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions sickness spreading. Verse 31 gives God's reason: “…so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them.” That's the stated reason, so that's the one to hold onto. I'd be careful about adding reasons of our own.

explanations.answer: So the nations around them stay far away
explanations.explanation: The nations don't come up in this verse. God's reason is: “…so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them.” (Leviticus 15:31). It's about His tabernacle and the people living near it. That's the reason the text gives.
Not at all. God calls it “My tabernacle, which is among them.” (Leviticus 15:31). It's not far off. It's right in the middle of the people.
Right, it's false. God says, “…My tabernacle, which is among them.” (Leviticus 15:31). So His tabernacle sits right in the middle of His people. I think that's the best part of the whole verse.
Yes, it's true. Verse 33 lists “…any male or female who has a discharge…” So the law covers both men and women. The list is long, and nobody is left out.
It's actually true. Verse 33 includes “…any male or female who has a discharge…” So the law covers men and women both. Nobody's left off the list.
